tldr: To solve the frequent configuration drift and reproducibility failures in swarm robotics reinforcement learning, the authors propose "MARGoS," a lightweight platform that systematically manages configuration hashing, seed propagation, and experiment bundles, demonstrating reduced manual effort and 100% reproducibility in the same environment.
overview:
In swarm robotics, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is gaining significant traction to acquire coordinated behaviors across large robot swarms. The large-scale simulator ARGoS is widely used for training, but simulator configuration XMLs, training scripts, random seeds, and environment parameters have traditionally been managed separately. As a result, issues like "the results do not reproduce even when running the exact same code" and "handoffs to other researchers fail" have been routine everyday problems both within and outside research labs.

To address this, the authors developed "MARGoS," a configuration-driven framework that takes the experiment-defining inputs away from individual user diligence and manages them as platform-level responsibilities. It integrates configuration hashing and frozen (immutable) configurations, end-to-end random seed propagation, environment fingerprinting, and an export/import bundle feature that includes the source code itself into a single pipeline.

The authors evaluated the platform across five rigorous dimensions: architecture, operational efficiency, reproducibility, analytical usability, and collaboration (handoff). Compared to manual workflows, MARGoS reduced operator time by 78.2% and achieved a 100% reproduction rate on the same hardware. While also revealing an inherent trade-off in the form of validation overhead during initial handoff, it presents a robust foundation pattern for guaranteeing reproducibility in simulation experiments.
contributions: Building an end-to-end integrated pipeline connecting ARGoS and MARL (RLlib/PettingZoo) that handles everything from configuration and execution to analysis and export.
Achieving reproducibility management that does not rely on individual discipline by introducing configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, and environment fingerprinting.
Enabling safe, asynchronous handoffs to others through self-contained experiment bundles that package source code and configurations together.
Defining a 5-dimension evaluation protocol quantifying operator time, keystrokes (KLM model), and reproduction rates, demonstrating the platform's effectiveness and its trade-offs with overhead.

sections.heading: Solving the everyday reproducibility crisis in swarm robotics with a platform
sections.summary: In swarm robotics MARL experiments, reproducibility breakdowns caused by manual management of simulator configurations, training code, and seed values are a severe challenge. MARGoS tackles this problem not by proposing a new learning algorithm, but as an infrastructure that governs experiment artifacts at the platform level.
sections.details:
In swarm robotics, where many simple autonomous robots gather and cooperate, training real physical hardware across dozens of robots takes far too much cost and time. Therefore, simulation-based training is the standard, and ARGoS-based MARL (ARGoS+MARL) is widely used.

However, this experimental workflow has a major trap. In practice, running a single experiment requires researchers to manually align ARGoS XML scenario files, RL training scripts, parameters, random seeds, and output paths. Because of this, subtle edits to configuration files or misconfigured seeds can silently alter the experiment, making reproduction and handoffs difficult even within the same research group.

The authors reframed this issue not as a question of "better algorithms," but as an "issue of configuration and reuse." The core philosophy is that the diverse inputs defining an experiment (artifacts) should be managed responsibly by the platform, rather than being left to the personal diligence of researchers.

The scope of MARGoS is very clear. It does not propose a new reinforcement learning algorithm; instead, it focuses on integrating configuration hashing, seed propagation, frozen (immutable) configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable bundles. The evaluation is clearly structured around five dimensions—architecture (RQ1), efficiency (RQ2), self-reproducibility (RQ3), usability (RQ4), and collaboration (RQ5)—to verify its real-world effectiveness as an experimental foundation.

sections.heading: Managing the complete experiment lifecycle with just five commands
sections.summary: MARGoS organizes the workflow from configuration to handoff into a 5-stage pipeline, designed to be operated via CLI with just five verb commands. ARGoS and Python-side RL environments are bridged via ZeroMQ using ArgosToZoo.
sections.details:
The architecture of MARGoS is simple and elegant. It defines the experiment workflow as a 5-stage pipeline: configuration $\to$ orchestration $\to$ logging $\to$ analysis $\to$ export/import.

Compared to prior platforms (such as systems using Robotarium, IsaacSim, or Alchemist), no previous system has specifically targeted ARGoS while covering this entire experiment lifecycle and experiment bundle exchange within a single framework.

The CLI (command line interface) presented to the user is stripped of unnecessary complexity, centered around five key verbs:
- run: loads configuration, propagates seeds, executes the run, and records step-level logs in a single stroke
- show: inspects details of saved run results
- compare: compares saved logs and configuration hashes to verify differences
- export: outputs a distributable bundle containing configurations, code, and logs
- import: ingests an external bundle and unpacks it into a reproducible state

A key design choice here is that there is no dedicated "reproduce" command. To reproduce a run, one simply imports the bundle, executes "run", and checks the output against the original using "compare".

To bridge the simulator and the training script, MARGoS adopts "ArgosToZoo". ARGoS and the Python environment communicate via ZeroMQ (a fast messaging library), exposing a PettingZoo-compatible interface that RL libraries like RLlib can consume directly.

Configuration management is equally critical. At runtime, the configuration is normalized, hashed, and stored as an immutable "frozen configuration". When generating a bundle for external sharing, referenced scenario files and the training code itself are bundled along, and file paths are automatically rewritten upon import. This ensures identical reproduction without being broken by changes in the sender's local directory paths.

sections.heading: Measuring platform performance with four objective, quantitative metrics
sections.summary: Platform evaluation was conducted based on objective measurements with pre-registered target thresholds (operator time, step counts, reproduction errors, KLM modeling, etc.). Subjective assessments like user surveys were intentionally excluded in favor of a fair, rigorous protocol.
sections.details:
To objectively prove the utility of the platform, the authors designed a rigorous evaluation protocol where evaluation metrics, passing thresholds, and sample sizes were frozen before experiments began. Subjective impression ratings, such as user surveys, were intentionally avoided.

The specific validation setups (RQ2 to RQ5) are as follows:

### Efficiency (RQ2)
Human operator time (measured via screen recordings) and operational steps required to run an experiment and extract results were compared between the manual baseline and MARGoS. Computation wait times were excluded to isolate pure human interaction costs. The target was a 50% or greater reduction in operator time and steps.

### Self-Reproducibility (RQ3)
A baseline experiment was re-run 20 times on the exact same hardware to test whether the final reward and the area under the learning curve (AUC) fell within $\pm 1\%$ of the baseline. The target was a success rate of 90% or higher.

### Analytical Usability (RQ4)
To eliminate developer subjectivity, Nielsen-style heuristic evaluations (35 items) and GOMS/KLM (Keystroke-Level Model: a mathematical model predicting expert task execution time from keystrokes and mouse actions) were used. The targets were a 50% or greater reduction in KLM predicted time across 7 representative tasks, and an 80% or higher heuristic compliance rate.

### Collaboration and Handoff (RQ5)
This scenario simulated handing off an experiment to an isolated environment set up for another user (with a separate home directory and shared virtual environment). Steps to share, sharing time, and reproduction time were measured, with handoff success defined as final rewards matching within $\pm 1\%$. Targets were a 50% or greater reduction across all durations and a 100% reproduction success rate.

sections.heading: Operator time down 78%, reproducibility hits 100%—and a clear trade-off emerges
sections.summary: Experimental results demonstrated drastic reductions in manual labor and achieved perfect reproducibility, clearing most preset targets. Meanwhile, they also revealed a realistic trade-off: safe handoff verification causes minor overhead during initial runs.
sections.details:
The measurements taken under the strict pre-registered criteria clearly show both the benefits and the real-world trade-offs of adopting the platform.

### Dramatic reduction in operator time and effort (RQ2)
The human operator time required to complete the baseline task plummeted from $87.0\pm 15.02$ seconds manually to $19.0\pm 1.41$ seconds with MARGoS—a 78.2% reduction (Mann–Whitney $U=0, p=0.011$). Interaction steps were reduced from 6.0 to 2.0 steps (a 66.7% reduction), easily surpassing the 50% target. Rather than altering training code, automating the manual handoffs across multiple tools delivered this substantial time saving.

### Flawless self-reproducibility (RQ3)
Across 20 re-runs on identical hardware, final rewards and AUC matched the baseline perfectly in every single execution (100% success rate, standard deviation 0.0000). System-enforced configuration hash verification and deterministic seed propagation proved capable of completely eliminating reproducibility failures caused by human error.

### Usability gains and boundaries (RQ4)
Heuristic compliance reached 85.7% (30/35 items), and weighted KLM-predicted execution time was reduced by 56.9%, both meeting their targets. Looking across tasks, however, clear boundaries emerge. Tasks involving execution, monitoring, and exporting (T3–T7) saw 58% to 88% reductions, whereas configuration editing tasks (T1–T2) saw a 0% reduction because parameters are still edited manually in a text editor. This shows an honest, natural boundary: usability only improves where the platform actually takes over the work.

### Handoff success and initial overhead (RQ5)
Handoff success reached 100% (10/10) for both manual and platform workflows. Steps required to share dropped by 87.5% (from 8 to 1), and sharing time dropped 65.3% (from $107.7\pm 24.1$ seconds to $37.4\pm 18.2$ seconds). However, reproduction time on the receiving end dropped by 45.9% (from $122.3\pm 30.3$ seconds to $66.2\pm 13.1$ seconds), falling just short of the 50% target. Furthermore, the first run on the platform side was actually 7.4% slower (56.5 seconds vs. 52.6 seconds).

This delay stems from bundle unarchiving, dynamic configuration path rewriting, and environment fingerprint integrity checks (such as verifying dependency packages). It provides a valuable practical lesson: robust, verified handoffs inevitably introduce validation overhead as an engineering trade-off.

sections.heading: How far can these results be trusted? Limitations and transferability
sections.summary: Limitations of this study include its single-evaluator self-assessment and a scope restricted to identical hardware and software stacks. However, the underlying architectural design—managing configurations and seeds at the platform level—is fully transferable to other simulators.
sections.details:
The authors openly address the limitations of their work through the lens of standard software engineering validities (internal, construct, external, and conclusion validity).

Regarding internal validity, the evaluation was conducted by the developer (self-evaluation). While measurements were automated and objective, operator familiarity bias cannot be entirely ruled out.

Regarding construct validity, usability was evaluated using expert KLM mathematical modeling and heuristic auditing rather than observing novice user behavior. It does not capture where beginners might stumble or make errors.

Regarding external validity, the study was limited to the ARGoS and RLlib combination, and reproducibility was verified strictly on the same machine. Portability across disparate operating systems or GPU environments is not guaranteed.

Nevertheless, the architectural design patterns demonstrated here—explicit configuration, deterministic seed propagation, structured logging, and exportable bundles—offer valuable, directly transferable blueprints for any workflow coupling reinforcement learning with other robotics simulators like IsaacLab or Gazebo.

sections.heading: A concrete first step toward ending ad-hoc experiment management
sections.summary: MARGoS consolidates the scattered components of ARGoS+MARL experiments into a single, cohesive pipeline. Future work will focus on cutting import validation overhead and expanding toward cross-platform portability across laboratories.
sections.details:
MARGoS transforms ARGoS+MARL experimental workflows, which previously relied heavily on human memory and diligence, into a configuration-driven pipeline that anyone can operate safely.

The findings are distinct. It reduced routine manual operator time by 78.2% and achieved perfect reproducibility (100% success rate) on the same machine. While enabling secure handoffs via distributable bundles, it also highlighted the realistic cost of initial validation overhead.

Looking forward, the authors plan to streamline import verification to reduce overhead, and extend these established management patterns to achieve full portability across different simulation environments and research labs. For any robotics researcher wrestling with messy day-to-day experiment management, this offers a compelling model.

takeaways: Relying on researcher diligence for reproducibility is fragile; platform-enforced configuration hashing and deterministic seed propagation are highly effective.
Systematically unifying simulator configurations, training code, and output paths cuts routine experimental operator time by roughly 80%.
Achieving safe, verified experiment handoffs through bundling incurs an inherent trade-off in the form of initial unpacking and environment-checking overhead.
limitations: The evaluation was a single-evaluator self-assessment by the developer, leaving novice error rates and learning curves unverified.
Reproducibility was evaluated solely on identical hardware; cross-platform reproducibility across different OSs or machines is not guaranteed.
Manual editing of configuration files (tasks T1–T2) is not automated, leaving manual labor costs intact for those initial steps.
